clue.text: Popular stop to applaud pilgrimage involving mass anointing

parts.note: to applaud is to clap

indicators.note: involving means the pilgrimage word holds the mass letter inside it

parts.note: the hajj (also spelt haj) is the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca
M is the abbreviation for mass in physics
unction is the act of anointing with oil

explanation.surface: Someone stops off to cheer on a pilgrimage that includes a service with holy oil.
explanation.walkthrough: CLAPHAM JUNCTION is a very busy London railway interchange, hence a popular stop. 'involving' puts M inside HAJ.
explanation.definitionFit: The busy south London railway station is a stop used by huge numbers of travellers.

clue.text: Not hard to ditch ageing fool of a husband

indicators.note: Not means the hard letter is left out of the ditch word

parts.note: to chuck is to ditch or throw away
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
ageing means old

explanation.surface: An elderly fool is not tough enough to dump his husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' removes H (hard) from CHUCK, leaving CUCK.
explanation.definitionFit: A man whose wife is unfaithful is traditionally mocked as a fool deceived by her.

clue.text: Phenomena ultimately hard to believe in any way

indicators.note: ultimately means the last letter of phenomena is taken

parts.note: a tall story is one hard to believe

explanation.surface: Things that are, in the end, not credible in any form.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an intensifier meaning in any respect or to any degree, as in 'not at all'.

clue.text: Stir dye with blubber

parts.note: a hue is a colour, as given by a dye
and means with, along with
to blubber is to cry

explanation.surface: Mixing colour while weeping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stir' is a noun, a commotion, not the verb of mixing paint.
explanation.definitionFit: A hue and cry is a public outcry or commotion, which is a stir.

clue.text: Girl overwhelmed by flash American charm

parts.note: a mo (moment) is a flash, as in 'in a flash'
Jo is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl swept off her feet by a showy American's charm.
explanation.definitionFit: Mojo is American slang for a magic charm or personal magnetism.

clue.text: Shoot films worth shooting

parts.note: U and PG are British film classifications, so films can be U and PG

indicators.note: shooting means the letters of worth are sent flying into a new order

parts.note: the letters of worth are the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A shoot of films that are worth making.
explanation.walkthrough: U (universal) and PG (parental guidance) are UK film ratings. 'shooting' rearranges WORTH as ROWTH.
explanation.definitionFit: An upgrowth is something that grows upwards, such as a plant's shoot.

clue.text: Fish daily in sound

indicators.note: in sound means the word for daily is heard spoken

parts.note: a daily or char is a British cleaning lady who comes in daily

explanation.surface: A newspaper about fishing, healthy and robust.
explanation.walkthrough: A daily is a British term for a cleaner, also a char; the fish is spelt CHARR as well as char.
explanation.definitionFit: The charr is a trout-like freshwater fish of cold northern lakes.

clue.text: Do keys quickly turn up in one's skip?

indicators.note: in means the turn-up word sits inside the other pieces

parts.note: one is I, so one's is I'S
to skip is to hop
to land is to arrive or turn up

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether their keys will show up in their rubbish skip.
explanation.walkthrough: Keys are low islands, as in the Florida Keys; to visit many in quick succession is to go from one to the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Island-hopping is travelling quickly between islands, and keys are small low islands.

clue.text: Delivering lad fresh ASBO not a difficulty ultimately

parts.note: fresh means new

indicators.note: not means the a is left out of ASBO
ultimately means the last letter of difficulty is taken

explanation.surface: A youth given a new antisocial behaviour order finds it no problem in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: An ASBO was a British Anti-Social Behaviour Order, a court order against nuisance conduct.
explanation.definitionFit: A newsboy is a boy who delivers newspapers.

clue.text: Irish county judge boarding Yank vessel for Bordeaux

parts.note: Clare is a county in the west of Ireland

indicators.note: boarding means the judge letter gets on board, inside the word for yank

parts.note: to yank is to tug

explanation.surface: An Irish judge climbs aboard an American ship carrying wine for Bordeaux.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank' looks like an American but is the verb, TUG. 'boarding' puts J inside TUG to make TJUG.
explanation.definitionFit: A claret jug is a decanter for red wine from Bordeaux, which the British call claret.

clue.text: Gleaming precious metal — blue

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver, a precious metal
blue means low in spirits, depressed

explanation.surface: A shiny piece of precious metal tinged with blue.
explanation.definitionFit: Something aglow is glowing, giving off a gleam of light.

clue.text: Old online diary retaining name in book form?

indicators.note: retaining means the diary word keeps the name letter held inside it

parts.note: a blog is an online diary

explanation.surface: An old internet diary is being kept with a name on it, perhaps to be printed as a book.
explanation.walkthrough: A book wider than it is tall is in oblong (landscape) format; the question mark flags this rather loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Oblong is a printers' term for a book whose pages are wider than they are tall, so a shape a book takes.

clue.text: Ball turning for opener

parts.note: a round knob that you twist to open something, read as a description of a household fitting rather than a dance or a cricket ball

explanation.surface: A cricket ball spinning to dismiss the opening batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture (a turning ball, an opening batsman) misleads: it is the round handle you turn to open a door.
explanation.definitionFit: The fitting is a ball-shaped handle that you turn to open a door, so a turning ball serves as an opener.

clue.text: Reason Dickens holds his head

indicators.note: holds means the word for Dickens contains the other piece inside it

parts.note: dickens and deuce are both old euphemisms for the devil, as in 'what the dickens/deuce'
his refers back to Dickens, whose head (first letter) is D

explanation.surface: The novelist Dickens keeps his head while thinking things through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dickens' looks like the novelist but is the euphemism for the devil, DEUCE; 'holds' puts D, the head of Dickens, inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To deduce is to work something out logically, which is to reason it through.

clue.text: Welsh community presenting log hewn in valley to the French

indicators.note: in means the rearranged log letters sit inside the valley word

parts.note: a dell is a small wooded valley

indicators.note: hewn means log is chopped and its letters rearranged

parts.note: the letters of log are the anagram fodder
au is French for to the

explanation.surface: A Welsh village shows off a chopped log in a valley, as the French would say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'presenting' is only a link word; the French for 'to the' supplies the final pair of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolgellau is a market town in Gwynedd, north Wales.

clue.text: Lytton and son attempt to conceal pain

indicators.note: to conceal means the attempt word hides the pain word inside it

parts.note: an attempt is a try
an ache is a pain

explanation.surface: Lytton and his son try to hide that they are hurting.
explanation.definitionFit: Lytton Strachey was the English biographer and Bloomsbury Group writer, so his first name identifies him.

clue.text: Starter none can follow for the present?

indicators.note: can follow means the none letter comes after the other piece

parts.note: being for the present is being against the past, anti past
O is zero, none

explanation.surface: An opener that nobody can top for a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: Anyone who is for the present can be thought of as anti the past; the question mark flags this whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasto is the Italian appetiser course served before the main meal.

clue.text: Impromptu crew operate lifting boxes in black out

indicators.note: lifting says the hidden letters are read backwards
boxes in means the words enclose the letters wanted

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An improvised team works hoisting crates during a blackout.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'boxes in black out' as the definition, but 'boxes in' is the hidden-word signal; the definition is 'black out'. In a down clue 'lifting' reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A power cut is a failure of electricity supply, which plunges places into a blackout.

clue.text: Wretched husband loves a fuss!

parts.note: bally is a dated British euphemism for bloody, meaning wretched or confounded
love is zero in tennis, written O, so two loves are OO

explanation.surface: A miserable husband enjoys making a scene.
explanation.walkthrough: BALLY is old British slang standing in for 'bloody'; 'loves' gives two Os since love means nil in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballyhoo is noisy commotion or publicity, much the same thing as a fuss.

clue.text: Homeless female happy shelter in inlet

indicators.note: shelter in means the happy word takes refuge inside the inlet word

parts.note: a bay is an inlet of the sea
glad means happy

explanation.surface: A homeless woman is pleased to find shelter in a bay.
explanation.definitionFit: A bag lady is a homeless woman who carries her possessions in bags.

clue.text: Approach rejected by heartless dummies

indicators.note: rejected means the remaining letters are turned back to front
heartless means one of the two middle letters of the dummies word is removed

parts.note: puppets are dummies, as a ventriloquist's dummy is

explanation.surface: A suitor's advance is spurned by some cruel idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' removes a central P from PUPPETS, giving PUPETS; 'rejected' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: To step up is to come forward or move closer, which is to approach.

clue.text: Locks put on cable rising in gorge

indicators.note: in means the cable piece goes inside the gorge word

parts.note: to gorge is to pig, as in pig out

indicators.note: rising, in a down clue, means the cable word reads upwards

parts.note: a cable is a wire

explanation.surface: Someone fixes locks onto a cable climbing through a ravine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gorge' is the verb (to eat greedily), not a ravine. 'rising' turns WIRE into ERIW.
explanation.definitionFit: A periwig is a wig, false locks of hair that one puts on.

clue.text: Eager beavers carrying light back in hazy sphere

indicators.note: carrying means the rearranged letters hold the next piece inside them
beavers is a verb here: the letters work busily and get rearranged

parts.note: the letters of eager are the anagram fodder

indicators.note: back means the light word is read backwards

parts.note: a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: Keen workers are carrying a lamp at the back of a fog-bound area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eager beavers' reads as one stock phrase, but 'beavers' is a verb (works busily) signalling the rearrangement of 'Eager'.
explanation.definitionFit: A grey area is a field where things are unclear, a vague or ill-defined domain.

clue.text: Cheers and riles us alternately

indicators.note: alternately means every other letter of and riles us is taken, starting with the first

explanation.surface: Applause and annoyance take turns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' is the British informal goodbye, not applause.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheers is informal British for goodbye, and adieu is a farewell.

clue.text: Run with speed — after a second one creates gap

indicators.note: after means the run and speed pieces follow the second

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
pace is speed
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A sprinter dashing off just after another, opening up a lead.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists the run and speed first, but 'after' puts them behind S.
explanation.definitionFit: A spacer is something inserted to keep two parts a set distance apart, so it makes a gap.

clue.text: Bones make beef inedible in the first place

parts.note: to beef is to complain, to carp

indicators.note: in the first place means the first letter of inedible is taken

explanation.surface: Bones are what make beef unfit to eat to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beef' is the verb to complain, not meat.
explanation.definitionFit: The carpi are the small bones of the wrist; carpus is the singular.

clue.text: One holding up English bank on Clydeside

parts.note: a bra is a garment that holds up the bust

explanation.surface: Someone propping up an English bank in Glasgow.
explanation.walkthrough: Clydeside is the area around Glasgow, so the word is Scots; 'bank' means a hillside, not a lender.
explanation.definitionFit: Brae is the Scots word for a hillside or slope, a bank of ground.

clue.text: Pound fine imposed on Bill Stevenson

indicators.note: imposed on means the pound and fine pieces are placed after the bill

parts.note: an ad (advertisement) is a bill, as in a poster
L is the abbreviation for pound, from the Latin libra
A1 means first-rate or fine, written here with letter I for the figure one

explanation.surface: A pound penalty is slapped on someone called Bill Stevenson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill Stevenson' looks like one name; the definition is just 'Stevenson' and 'Bill' is AD. A1 is written AI in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Adlai Stevenson was the American politician twice nominated for president, so his first name points to him.

clue.text: Graves opened by this city's gang

parts.note: Cork is a city in Ireland, so the city's is Cork's
a crew is a gang

explanation.surface: Graves are dug open by a local gang in this town.
explanation.walkthrough: Graves here is a red or white Bordeaux wine, not a burial plot; 'this' in the definition points to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bottle of Graves, a Bordeaux wine, is opened with a tool that draws out its cork.

clue.text: There's no way children should go about flying jumbo kites!

indicators.note: go about means the children word surrounds the rearranged letters

parts.note: the young are children, offspring

indicators.note: flying means the letters of jumbo kites are tossed about and rearranged

parts.note: the letters of jumbo kites are the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Disbelief that children ought to be let loose with giant kites.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumbo' suggests a jet but is simply fodder alongside 'kites'; 'children' is the outer piece, split round the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation expresses flat disbelief, a colloquial equivalent of saying something cannot be so.
